Missing data hinder replication of artificial intelligence studies

The problem of replication is quite different from what we see in psychology, though. Unlike psychology or social science it's not because studies are rubbish designed to support a theory that you had before starting, but due to some inherent properties of the field, combined with a high profitability of this research:

  1. There is a lot of uncertainty and randomness in all AI algorithms. Some people have enough experience and intuition to design proper algorithms and fine-tune meta parameters, but except this very small group, everyone playing with the AI uses the approach of "throw everything at the wall and see what sticks".
  2. Licenses - if you use something that you're not supposed to use without paying a bazillion of dollars, then you won't share your source code, you'll just share some pseudocode, results and handwave everything else.
  3. Data - collecting/tagging enough meaningful data to train algorithms properly is time consuming, and expensive. Not everyone is going to share it for free or almost free. Actually the availability of good datasets is the biggest limiting factor when you're starting a new project.
  4. People who get good results in profitable fields will not be eager to share too many details, people who get a decent result once per every 100 tries, will not share too many details either.
